newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian Metals - LME copper to drift in weak market.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals - LME copper to drift in weak market.

text.p: Copper will probably drift sideways on the London Metal Exchange (LME) near term as overall weak global demand undermines a revival in prices, regional traders said on Friday.

LME three-month copper dropped to a two-month low of $1,840 a tonne on Thursday before recovering to a close at $1,852. The red metal was being quoted at $1,852/58 a tonne at 0300 GMT in Asia on Friday.
"The market's just going to drift. There's no reason for it to rebound," a senior trader at a Singapore-based firm said.
"I feel the weakness will continue to prevail in the market. Demand is weak and prices will probably move sideways. I don't really see the market heading up," he added.
But another trader said the recent fall in copper may lure some buyers bargain-hunting after the sharp drop in prices.

"I have a feeling prices will go up this afternoon," said the trader in a Japanese metal company. He said, however, any bounce will be small and that three-month copper may reach about $1,870/75 a tonne.
Indonesia and Malaysia were still in the market for about 700 tonnes of copper, but some of their buyers find Singapore copper premiums too steep for comfort, traders said.
Singapore copper premiums over LME cash metal hovered almost unchanged at $100 to $115 a tonne, buoyed by good demand.
"The Malaysians were looking for 300-400 tonnes, but I don't think they've gotten it yet," one dealer said.
"Those buyers are being discouraged by the high premiums here," another trader said.
Chinese buyers, currently sated with copper imports, have practically disappeared from the market, traders said.

China's imports of copper and copper alloys from January to July soared 84.4 percent to 128,000 tonnes against the same period last year while copper profile imports climbed 15.2 percent to 215,300 tonnes, the China Daily said on Thursday.
"The Chinese have dropped out of sight and it may take some time for them to come back because of the imports they have taken in," one dealer said.
Asian demand for aluminium, especially in Japan, has picked up although the falling price of the metal has made it difficult for some dealers to conclude deals.

"I was just about to fix the price for some aluminium from Australia, but the price would drop and the buyer would become skittish. I've been forced to park the ingots in the warehouse," one trader said.
Aluminium touched a two-year low at the LME on Thursday at $1,429 a tonne before recovering slightly to end at $1,434.
"Demand in Japan has definitely picked up. Material that used to wind up in Singapore is ending up in Japan. Eventually, this may cause premiums here to edge up," a Japanese trader said.
The LME stocks report due out at 0800 GMT could provide a few leads for the base metals market, but any impact will probably be short-lived, traders said.
"It's a weak market so the impact of the report may be quickly discounted," one dealer said.
